segments.text: We are {team_name}: {others} and me, Yash Goel.

Our dataset is GOES-16's lightning mapper. One file every 5 minutes through six years, 2019 to 2024, averaged to one typical year of {flashes_m} million sampled flashes on a 1 degree grid by hour and season.
First, where. Land dominates: {land_share:.0f} percent of flashes, hotspots: Lake Maracaibo, northern Colombia, the Amazon, the Gulf coast.
Second, when. Lightning peaks at {all_peak}; 1 to 6 PM holds {all_afternoon:.0f} percent of all flashes.
Third, land against ocean. Land peaks at {land_peak}, ocean at {ocean_peak}, and {ocean_night:.0f} percent of ocean flashes happen at night.

Fourth, each cell's peak hour. {land_aft:.0f} percent of land cells peak in the afternoon, {ocean_night_cells:.0f} percent of ocean cells at night. The Great Plains are the evening patch inside a continent.
Fifth, three regions. The Southeast peaks at {se_peak}, the Amazon at {amazon_peak}, but the Plains at {plains_peak}, {plains_night:.0f} percent of it at night.

Sixth, six years, one shape. Land peaked at {land_peak} in all six years; the ocean peak drifts between {ocean_lo} and {ocean_hi} on a curve that is nearly flat overnight. A climatology, not one year's weather.

segments.item: Title of the graph and the question
segments.text: Our title: {title}. Our question: at what hour does lightning peak over land and ocean, and where does it strike at night?

segments.item: Current progress on the final dynamic graph
segments.text: Our D3 prototype: play the hour and watch land light up by afternoon, the sea by night. Switch season or clock, click two cells, read the six-year chart underneath. Left: polish and the write-up.
